messages.author: ee3aa4887fb0b91c
messages.subject: Coverage - beta expectation
parts:
Hello,

Best wishes first to your incredible team !

Some months ago, I came up with having different results when using different parametrizations of the same model (mainly, in term of sd and in term of precision = 1/sd^2). I realised at this time that intervals obtained with the "sd" parametrization were extremely large when degrees of freedom (df) were low, for both the parameters and the predictions (beta-expectation tolerance intervals). When I said "large" at this time, I already meant "larger than what is expected because of low df".

At the time, we had some discussion on priors, on Jacobians, on some additional good advice for model implementation, etc., and the last point not yet discussed was to check carefully the coverage; namely, to see if the obtained prediction intervals were of expectation beta (if beta is the expected coverage).

So, I did the simulations. Here, with a simple linear regression (assume it is a model for a variable recorded along the time). I'll look at the coverage for the prediction of a single time point. I fixed beta at 95% (because as a statistician, I cannot come with a better idea :-D ), and I looked at the expected/average coverage across all simulations.

Four files are attached, all self running (data are generated each time):
- Frequentist classical prediction interval (i.e. the beta-expectation tolerance interval, in this case)
- MCMCregress (package MCMCpack) implementation of the same.
- Stan implementation of the same with uniform prior (I also try with other implementations, e.g. centred X, as done with brms package.), and inv_gamma [message edited to add it]. Might be better with inv_gamma prior for support, but uniform shouldn't lead to that much trouble.

For Bayesian framework, again, I tried to be non informative with Stan, i.e. using improper uniform prior. Indeed, in a simulation exercise, I don't want to / cannot use as prior what I know from my simulated data. Similar for inv_gamma prior. For MCMCregress, I did not specify any prior (I let the default, which is similar to one would assumed non-informative with conjugate prior, i.e. inverse_gamma(0.0001,0.0001) for sigma^2).

Results are all good for both the Frequentist estimates and Bayesian MCMCregress results (on plots, blue line must be on top of the red line, located at beta=95% coverage). However, Stan coverages with uniform priors are over-estimated when df are low (i.e. blue line higher than red line in small df cases, i.e. not of beta-expectation). This is really embarrassing as small data remains the common place in many domains. From previous experiments, all other Gibbs or M-H based samplers perform better with low df (but really I like Stan language and flexibilities so much... :-) ). Stan is "stabilized" with inv_gamma prior, but coverage are always "just a little bit too low". I would have preferred the opposite :-s. 

I did not check precisely, but I am sure that the posterior distribution of the parameters does not exhibit good coverage properties in the uniform case (the predictive only borrows their own variabilities). It would mean the exploration of the posterior distribution with NUTS has some trouble here.

Fortunately, most user of samplers tend to be careful with the use of their results. But this type of issue seems more difficult to handle and detect, in my opinion (in my case, on the previous posts (see link above), intervals were so large that I did not believe in them, and I had Frequentist approximations to figure it out, but in some cases... well... it might be dangerous). 
Fortunately, again, these results are conservative (intervals too large), which in most of the time protect the statistician, but not always as with the inverse gamma.

Any idea of what would cause that and if there is a way, or a plan, to improve/correct that ?

Also, keep up with the awesome work up to there. 

Kind regards,
-----------
Pierre

ps: try to run the code with Stan twice in a row. On my machine, R crashes completely the second time, at the time of model compilation... That's probably a problem with parallelism, but the way it is done (Stan not in parallel, simulations in parallel) is the fastest I've found.

messages.author: ee3aa4887fb0b91c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Coverage - beta expectation
parts:
Hi Daniel,

In the first post of this thread, you will see 4 R files, which are stand-alone, with stan code (for the one made with Stan) and simulations (which contains generated data).

To understand as fast as possible, I suggest you to look at the files 
- coverage regression Bayesien Stan for Stangroup.R
- coverage regression Freq for Stangroup.R

In these files, for a simple regression, I am computing predictive distributions on which I take the quantiles, which basically are beta-expectation tolerance intervals. So, my point is to verify if, on average during the simulation, the coverage is beta. Classical check.

When degrees of freedom are low, coverages obtained in Stan are not good (intervals are too large). I can compare to the Frequentist solution (lm(...) and predict.lm(...) with intervals="prediction") to make an idea. These ones are perfectly aligned with the expectations. (I also compared to classical Gibbs sampler MCMCregress, in another file, also attached,which is working better than Stan, for this example).

My other concern is that the chains does not look particulary bad, and no other convergence and sampler behavior metrics allows me detecting issues. The only thing I know is that the model is "hard" because of low data point, and the uniform prior is not always the best option (but in a simulation setting, I really want to be that non-informative). I also know that I could slightly improve the model by scaling and centering the X. I tried it as well, but then removed it because it does not change the results, and so the model is much more readable for you guys.

Finally, I know that, with low d.f., the posterior distribution of sigma is probably awfully too variable and too close to 0, which make it not well defined (as it is the case with random models with few subjects). Still, on average, I would expect that my coverage would be of beta-expectation.

Thanks again to have a quick look on that.

Kind regards,

Pierre

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Coverage - beta expectation
parts:
Uniform priors are not "uninformative". They have
an implied scale. For instance, uniform on a
probability in (0, 1) is logistic on the log odds of
that probability.

You should get coverage in the Bayesian sense that
if you simulate from your model (not something like
your model, but really simulate from your model's priors)
then you should get 50% coverage by 50% intervals.
If you have improper priors, it's not really possible to
simulate properly from your model.

When you say MCMCregress is working better, what are
you considering better?

I also don't know what you mean in the earlier posts
that Stan is "stabilized" with an inverse gamma prior.

I didn't see the files you were talking about.

- Bob

However, Stan coverages with uniform priors are over-estimated when df are low (i.e. blue line higher than red line in small df cases, i.e. not of beta-expectation). This is really embarrassing as small data remains the common place in many domains. From previous experiments, all other Gibbs or M-H based samplers perform better with low df (but really I like Stan language and flexibilities so much... :-) ). Stan is "stabilized" with inv_gamma prior, but coverage are always "just a little bit too low". I would have preferred the opposite :-s.
>>
>> I did not check precisely, but I am sure that the posterior distribution of the parameters does not exhibit good coverage properties in the uniform case (the predictive only borrows their own variabilities). It would mean the exploration of the posterior distribution with NUTS has some trouble here.
>>
>> Fortunately, most user of samplers tend to be careful with the use of their results. But this type of issue seems more difficult to handle and detect, in my opinion (in my case, on the previous posts (see link above), intervals were so large that I did not believe in them, and I had Frequentist approximations to figure it out, but in some cases... well... it might be dangerous).
>> Fortunately, again, these results are conservative (intervals too large), which in most of the time protect the statistician, but not always as with the inverse gamma.
>>
>> Any idea of what would cause that and if there is a way, or a plan, to improve/correct that ?
>>
>> Also, keep up with the awesome work up to there.
>>
>> Kind regards,
>> -----------
>> Pierre
>>
>> ps: try to run the code with Stan twice in a row. On my machine, R crashes completely the second time, at the time of model compilation... That's probably a problem with parallelism, but the way it is done (Stan not in parallel, simulations in parallel) is the fastest I've found.

Hi Bob,

Thanks for your answer. That's true that I don't simulate from my Bayesian model, but from a much simpler generative Normal model with no prior involved. I wouldn't have think about that ! But then it also means that the simple linear model is poorly adapted to the data, even if the generative model doesn't look different (I am just creating a line and then add some variability around).

What I get here that if there is a very few data points, some weakly uninformative prior should really be set to get better posteriors, but I feel that's weird to do that in a simulation setting (here, data does not represent anything, so I would need to create the prior from the data, which I won't do !). Prior sensitivity here is huge, and this is not something I like or is easy to deal with, in many situations.

On a side, when I mentioned uniform prior, I meant that I just specified a positive support for the variance/sd parameter, and no upper bound, in the parameter block, and no further proper or improper distribution.
And when I said the word "stabilized", I meant that the posteriors were looking more as I would expect (that was a very poor wording from my side, sorry).

Thanks again,

Pierre

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Coverage - beta expectation
parts:
> On Feb 16, 2017, at 7:03 PM, Pierre Lebrun <lebrun...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
>
> Thanks for your answer. That's true that I don't simulate from my Bayesian model, but from a much simpler generative Normal model with no prior involved. I wouldn't have think about that ! But then it also means that the simple linear model is poorly adapted to the data, even if the generative model doesn't look different (I am just creating a line and then add some variability around).

The generative model does look different. The generative model defines
a density over the parameters, and that's what's different. It may feel
similar, but what you're seeing is real differences.

And you're right---the simple linear regression may not be well adapted
to your data. The model's definitely misspecified in the technical sense
if it doesn't match the data-generating process, so all the guarantees
about coverage go out the window. This means in practice you have to be more
careful validating on held out data to try to evaluate the sensitivity to
this misspecification (same way as you evaluate sensitivity to priors).
We like to use predictive posterior distributions.

> What I get here that if there is a very few data points, some weakly uninformative prior should really be set to get better posteriors, but I feel that's weird to do that in a simulation setting (here, data does not represent anything, so I would need to create the prior from the data, which I won't do !).

The data are supposed to represent what results from the generative
model you specify. The priors indicate the range the parameters can
take. If your inclination is to simulate from a narrow range and
have a prior that's huge relative to that narrow range of expected
or reasonable values, I'd suggest tightening your priors.
> Prior sensitivity here is huge, and this is not something I like or is easy to deal with, in many situations.

You may not like it, but if you don't have data, you can't infer from
thin air. If you only have a handful of data points, you want the
prior to contribute heavily in a hierarchical model to pull your estimate
toward a population mean (there are two case studies on the web site
from the documentation page on hierarchical models and why you want
to do this).

>
> On a side, when I mentioned uniform prior, I meant that I just specified a positive support for the variance/sd parameter, and no upper bound, in the parameter block, and no further proper or improper distribution.

That's improper. Meaning that it doesn't integrate to a finite value.
Stan requires the posterior to be proper. But if the prior is
very wide, you need more data to get a well-behaved posterior. Michael's
about to roll out a case study explaining this.
> And when I said the word "stabilized", I meant that the posteriors were looking more as I would expect (that was a very poor wording from my side, sorry).

That's fine---that's what I thought you meant. I don't think there's
a good noun for that. But it's part of the modeling process. You want
to make sure you're getting reasonable posteriors.

> Weird that you cannot see the files in the first post of the thread, they have very large icons within the text in the bottom. Maybe google group is messing something on your browser... I reattached the most important file here. If you have further advice on it, I am willing to take them :-)

Got it. The key part is the model:

data {
int<lower=1> N; // total number of observations
vector[N] Y; // response variable
int<lower=1> K; // number of population-level effects
matrix[N, K] X; // population-level design matrix
}
parameters {
vector[K] b; // population-level effects
real<lower=0> sigma; // residual SD
}
model {
vector[N] eta;
eta = X * b;
// likelihood contribution
Y ~ normal(eta, sigma);
}

I'd recommend indenting, but otherwise this is just a standard linear
regression with improper flat priors on coefficients and noise scale.

You may want to try simulating data and running maximum likelihood estimates
with something like lm() in R (essentially a bootstrap estimate of the variance
in the MLE).

- Bob
